A generation begins with three files: a style guide, a corpus passage, and a
prompt template. The runner parses the frontmatter of each, hashes the file
whole, and records the hash alongside the output. The guide's body becomes the
system prompt. The passage is substituted into the template to form the user
prompt, which is written to the child process on standard input rather than
passed as an argument, so that no shell quoting rule and no command-line length
limit ever applies to it. The runner then spawns the Claude Code CLI with an
explicit argument vector, requests a JSON envelope, and waits with a timeout
that escalates from a polite termination signal to a forced kill. What comes
back is parsed even when the process exits non-zero, because a refusal arrives
that way: a failing exit code and a well-formed envelope that names the reason.
Every field of that envelope is written to disk, successful or not, along with
the argument vector, the resolved model, the token counts, and the wall-clock
duration.
</passage>

response.text:
Each generation run starts with three inputs: a style guide, a sample passage, and a prompt template. The runner reads the frontmatter from each file, computes a hash of the entire file, and saves that hash together with the output. The text of the guide becomes the system prompt, while the passage gets inserted into the template to create the user prompt. That user prompt is sent to the child process through standard input instead of as a command-line argument, which means shell quoting rules and argument-length limits never come into play.

Next, the runner launches the Claude Code CLI using an explicit list of arguments, asks for output in JSON format, and waits for a response under a timeout scheme that starts with a gentle termination request and escalates to a forced kill if needed. The runner still parses the returned output even when the process ends with a non-zero exit code, since refusals show up exactly that way — a failing exit code paired with a properly formatted JSON envelope explaining why. Regardless of whether the run succeeded, every field from that envelope gets saved to disk, along with the argument list used, the model that was actually invoked, the token counts, and how long the whole thing took in real time.
